summary:
MoonBase Colony is a browser-based strategy game where players run a research outpost at the lunar south pole. Players build solar farms, batteries, ice extractors, oxygen generators, greenhouses and shielded habitats, then try to keep their crew alive through the long lunar night.

The challenge asks how people can learn the trade-offs of running a lunar outpost. In our game, those trade-offs are the gameplay. Power, oxygen, water, food, CO₂ and radiation all depend on each other. Solar power stops at night, regolith shielding costs material that buildings also need, and dust, micrometeoroids and solar storms force hard choices. Monitoring stations and a Mission Control center show live NASA space-weather data from DONKI and real lunar imagery from Moon Trek. The game always labels which values are real and which are simulated.

This matters because NASA’s Artemis program plans to return people to the Moon, and the next generation needs to understand why lunar engineering is hard. MoonBase Colony turns real science into decisions students make for themselves. It’s free, runs on phones, and saves progress to the cloud.
details:
What it does and how it works
MoonBase Colony is a free browser strategy game where you run a research outpost at the lunar south pole. You build solar farms, batteries, regolith mines, ice extractors, oxygen generators, greenhouses, habitats, a spaceport and a research lab. Builder robots construct and upgrade them over time. Everything runs on one connected simulation:

  • Solar power stops during the long lunar night, so batteries must carry the base until sunrise.
  • Ice becomes water or oxygen, but not both.
  • Crew members consume O₂, water and food and produce CO₂ and waste.
  • Solar storms raise the radiation dose unless habitats are shielded with regolith.

If any of these systems fails, crew health drops and the mission can end. A Mission Control center has four departments: Environment, Life Support, Power and Operations. Six dynamic events (solar storm, dust on panels, equipment failure, water leak, battery fault and loss of communications) pause the game, and you choose one of three responses. Each choice really changes the game state.

Benefits and intended impact
Space learning materials for students are often either too simple or too technical. Our game sits in the middle: students learn engineering trade-offs by making decisions and living with the consequences, not by memorising facts. It includes:

  • 20 science cards with sources and a 22-term glossary
  • A quiz every lunar sunrise and a mission report with feedback
  • 37 achievements, five story chapters and four difficulty levels

It runs on phones and computers with nothing to install, so it can be used in any classroom. With Artemis returning people to the Moon, we want young people to understand why living there is hard, and to get excited about solving those problems.

Tools and technologies

  • React and TypeScript, with Phaser 3 drawing the isometric map
  • Vite, Tailwind CSS and Vitest (83 automated tests, including balance tests on every difficulty)
  • Supabase for sign-in by email link and cloud saves, protected by Row Level Security
  • Vercel for hosting, deploying automatically from GitHub
    • DONKI: live solar flares that set storm strength
    • Moon Trek: an LRO map of the Moon
    • NTRS: technical reports, linked after events

We built it together with Claude (Claude Code), an AI assistant from Anthropic. Our team chose the idea, made the design decisions, play-tested the game and set up the services. Claude wrote most of the code and tests and helped find real facts and sources.

Creativity

  • All art, including buildings, rovers, craters and astronauts, is drawn in code, so it is fully original.
  • Real NASA space weather changes the game: when the real Sun is active, in-game storms get stronger.
  • The genre is the “build your base” style many students already love, but every rule comes from real physics.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: real values are labelled “Real science” with a source, and every simplification is labelled “Game assumption”. If NASA data is unavailable, the game falls back to a cached copy, then a bundled snapshot, and only then to simulated data, which is always marked as simulated.
  • Accessibility and devices: it works in a browser on computers and phones, with keyboard, mouse and touch.
  • Difficulty for different ages: four levels change the day/night length, build speed and resources.
  • Balance: the first lunar night has to be survivable on every difficulty, and automated tests check this.
  • Privacy and safety: saves work offline by default, cloud sign-in is optional and needs no password, and each player can only read their own save.
